chunks: Analog versus digital signals. The question: What is the difference between an analog signal and a digital signal?
An analog signal is continuous. At any instant it can take any value in a range, like the voltage from a microphone.
A digital signal takes only a limited set of values, often just two (high and low), and is read at specific times. A converter called an ADC turns analog into digital.
Digital signals resist noise, which is why computers use them.
Compare a ramp with a staircase. On a ramp you can stand at any height. On a staircase you can stand only on a step. Now suppose a little dust makes you wobble.
On the ramp, your height changes. On the staircase, you still stand on the same step. That is why digital survives noise that damages analog signals.
The dashed analog curve is defined everywhere.
The solid trace holds each sample for 1/12 seconds (sample-and-hold) and rounds it to one of 8 levels, which is what a 3-bit ADC followed by a DAC would produce.
The difference between the curves is the quantization error plus the time-discretization error.

Drag the bits to 1 and the staircase collapses to a two-level square wave; drag samples per cycle to 3 and the held steps barely resemble a sine, even though three samples per cycle is still above the Nyquist minimum of two.
Sampling: measuring a signal at regular instants in time. Quantization: rounding each measurement to the nearest of a fixed set of levels.
ADC (analog-to-digital converter): the circuit that samples and quantizes. Bit: one binary digit, 0 or 1. An N-bit converter has 2 to the N levels.
Noise margin: how much unwanted noise a digital signal can tolerate before it is misread.
Take a 12-bit ADC with a 3. 3 volts range. It has 2¹² = 4096 levels, so each step is 3. 3 ÷ 4096 about 0. 8 millivolts.
Rounding to the nearest level causes an error of up to half a step, and the typical error, averaged over many readings, is about 0. 23 millivolts. Each extra bit halves the step.
Now the noise margin. In classic 3. 3 volts logic, a driver outputs at least 2. 4 volts for "high", and a receiver accepts anything above 2. 0 volts as high. The margin is 0.
4 volts. Noise below 0. 4 volts causes no error at all. That is the whole idea.
"Analog signals are continuous in time and amplitude, like a microphone voltage.
Digital signals are discrete in both: sampled at intervals and quantized to a finite number of levels, usually represented as bits.
An ADC converts analog to digital, adding quantization error of about LSB over root 12.
Digital wins on noise immunity, because gates regenerate clean levels, and on storage and processing.
Analog is still needed at the interfaces, and real digital edges are analog waveforms."
